extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, curriculum researchers, and higher-education assessment designers evaluating calculus reform programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, conducting, and interpreting qualitative and quantitative assessment of undergraduate calculus reform programs (e.g., C4L, Project CALC), including study design, instrumentation, outcome measures, and implementation success factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual-method assessment (quantitative + qualitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use both quantitative and qualitative assessment methods in tandem: quantitative assessment provides somewhat objective numerical measures of success or failure and effectiveness across sub-populations; qualitative assessment aims to gain a more complete idea of what the student is actually thinking when struggling with material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative data outline effectiveness but offer few clues for directions for change; qualitative data, though subjective, are rich sources for ideas for improvement. Use both methods together to fine-tune course delivery and to clarify essential understandings and their development over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative assessment: common exam and statistical comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a standardized/final examination given to all comparison groups (reform and traditional) to provide an objective basis for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the exam to reflect skills emphasized in the comparison target; minimize grading variance by assigning faculty to grade specified questions across all sections. Use summary statistics (max, quartiles, median, min) and track percentile-range performance by semester to observe trends across cohorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative assessment: student interviews and classroom dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct in-depth interviews, classroom observations, and record frequent instructor/student dialogues to uncover students' mental models and how they interpret graphs, text, expressions, and notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid instructor assumptions about student interpretation; teach students to read/interpret mathematical artifacts; probe for misunderstandings such as pronoun references, implicit parentheses, and vocabulary differences. Use interview findings to generate curriculum/pedagogy improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic decomposition of concepts (qualitative research procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a genetic decomposition of each basic mathematical concept into developmental steps following a Piagetian theory of knowledge; hypothesize decompositions and modify them based on in-depth student interviews and observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and pilot interview protocols; conduct many interviews (C4L had over 125 on core concepts), transcribe interviews (transcription can take ~6 hours each), analyze iteratively, and use findings to modify curricular treatments and texts where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal study design with explanatory and response variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Design longitudinal comparisons of reform and traditional students using response variables (outcomes) and explanatory variables (controls) to allow meaningful comparisons despite self-selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where random assignment is impractical, use explanatory variables and linear models to control confounding and to perform matching-like comparisons so as to use all available data. Consult statistical experts when planning and analyzing such studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response variables for longitudinal evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Select clear outcome metrics such as: (1) number of calculus courses taken from first, second and third semester calculus; (2) number of mathematics courses taken beyond calculus; (3) average grade in calculus courses; (4) average grade in mathematics courses beyond calculus; (5) last available overall grade point average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model each response variable as a linear function of explanatory variables and perform statistical tests for significance; use these outcomes to answer programmatic questions about retention, subsequent course-taking, and grade performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory/control variables to include
rubrics_metrics.description: Include predictor/control variables that account for background and confounding factors: Predicted GPA (PGPA), indicator for missing PGPA, number of semesters since first calculus, major (engineering, math, science, other), interaction between semester and major, gender, and program indicator (C4L vs TRAD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute PGPA using available precollege measures (e.g., SAT verbal/math, average high school grades, percentile rank cubed); include interaction terms as needed; the linear model should test whether explanatory variables have statistically significant effects on each response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing self-selection and matching limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge self-selection bias as a limitation when students choose reform vs traditional; prefer random assignment when practical, but when not, use analytic methods to mitigate bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random assignment may be impractical due to dropout and awareness of differences; instead, use linear models with explanatory variables to effectively 'match' students with similar characteristics and use all available data rather than discarding large control samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACE learning cycle as course-structure criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure units around the Activity-Class-Exercise (ACE) cycle: begin with computer investigations in lab, follow with class meetings using a modified Socratic approach and cooperative problem solving, and finish with traditional exercises to reinforce constructed knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each ACE unit typically lasts about a week; labs help students construct meaning, classes help build on lab experiences, and exercises reinforce skills. This structure minimizes lecturing and emphasizes student construction of understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project/program learning goals (student competencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify explicit learning goals such as: using mathematics to structure and investigate real-world questions; using calculus to formulate, solve, and communicate problems; integrating technology into formulation/solution/communication; and learning to work cooperatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these competencies as targets for curriculum design, classroom activities, and for aligning assessment instruments (e.g., problem-solving tests, writing tasks, lab reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment instrument components (five-part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating outcomes, include a multi-part instrument assessing: attitudes, basic skills, writing, problem solving, and conceptual understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Project CALC: attitudes (agreement with statements about calculus use and understanding), skills (routine computations), writing (short essay illustrating derivative concept), problem solving (non-routine word problems), conceptual understanding (identify functions and derivatives from graphs). Consider fatigue effects when grouping subtests; administer appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative evaluation and observational methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use formative evaluation early: teach both experimental and traditional sections, observe classes regularly, hold discussions with regular student groups, read student comments, and hold conversations with faculty to identify strengths and problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formative methods reveal student engagement, morale, and early implementation problems; use findings to iterate on pedagogy and course design before summative comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading and scoring standardization
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardize grading to reduce instructor-to-instructor variance in assessment outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have each faculty member grade designated questions for all students across sections or otherwise centralize scoring procedures to make cross-section comparisons fairer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation success factors and instructor practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful implementation requires faculty time to understand student thinking, to design activities that replace naive models with appropriate ones, and to adapt syllabus and class time to support this development. Be patient, persevere, maintain humor, make no assumptions, be creative, and enjoy teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect a break-in/adaptation period (1.5–2 years) for experimental approaches to be adapted to local conditions. Anticipate student resistance; consider support measures (e.g., lab assistants) and balance student explorations with teacher-guided activities to improve morale and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource and labor expectations for qualitative research
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan for substantial time and resources: design and pilot interviews, pay participants if necessary, transcribe interviews (approx. six hours each), and allocate substantial researcher-hours for analysis and write-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train researchers in qualitative procedures; consider hiring/transcription support; video increases time/cost. The process contributes to pedagogical design and professional development but should not be undertaken lightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of follow-up and retention studies as outcome measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess longer-term impacts via retention studies and follow-up comparisons: test sophomores/juniors on writing, skills, problem solving, concepts, and attitudes; analyze whether experimental students take/do better in subsequent courses requiring calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use matched-pair interviews and follow-up grade analyses to understand persistence of effects; be aware of selection and participation rates when interpreting results.
